name: Status Quo Bias
description: People disproportionately prefer to keep things the way they are, even when a switch would be objectively beneficial and low-cost.
design_relevance_note: The psychological mechanism underlying why smart defaults are so effective in onboarding and settings design.
prevalence_note: Recognized in choice-architecture discourse, but usually discussed as a close cousin of the more commonly-invoked Default Effect rather than cited independently as often.

findings.description: Across 58 default studies (pooled n = 73,675), pre-selected options raised selection with a considerable average effect (d = 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.83) but with substantial variation: most studies found positive effects, several found none, and two found negative effects. Defaults were more effective in consumer domains and less effective in environmental ones, and more effective when seen as endorsement or as reflecting the status quo (endowment).
findings.source_title: When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects

findings.description: Across multiple decision contexts, including real employee retirement/benefits-plan choices, people show a significant, persistent bias toward maintaining the current/default option even when objectively superior alternatives are available and switching costs are trivial.
findings.source_title: Status quo bias in decision making

applications.title: A subscription-service firm proactively recommending cost-minimising plans to customers, which increased churn
applications.description: In a large-scale field experiment, some customers of a service firm were offered recommendations to switch to cost-minimising pricing plans and others were not. Contrary to the expectation that customers on a suitable plan would be less likely to leave, those who received the recommendation churned more. The authors propose two explanations that the data support: the campaign lowered customers' inertia to switch plans, and it raised the salience of past-usage patterns among potential churners. The abstract does not name the firm or its sector.
applications.industry_context: subscription service with pricing plans (firm and sector not named in the abstract)
applications.ethical_note: The recommendations pointed customers to plans that minimised their own cost, so the campaign served customers' interests, and the firm's loss from it shows that helping customers was not free for the business. The ethical risk is in what firms may conclude: that such help should be dropped or hidden because it raises churn. The paper's own recommendation is to target such campaigns more carefully, not to abandon them.

applications.title: Adobe's renewal email obscuring subscription cost, date, and cancellation path
applications.description: Adobe's subscription renewal email conceals the renewal cost, the renewal date, and a clear path to cancel -- relying on customers' natural tendency to stay with the current arrangement (inaction) rather than requiring a deliberate choice to continue.
applications.ethical_note: Concealing the specific information a customer would need to make a deliberate renewal decision -- cost, date, and how to opt out -- is a direct match for this corpus's existing dark-patterns literature on obscured cancellation paths, not an ambiguous edge case.

applications.title: Amazon's Subscribe & Save discount overcoming resistance to recurring purchases
applications.description: Amazon offers a 5-15% discount for enrolling a product in its Subscribe & Save recurring-delivery program, using a concrete financial incentive to make switching away from one-time purchases (the status quo for most shoppers) feel worthwhile.
applications.ethical_note: The discount is a real, transparent, and unconditional financial benefit disclosed upfront -- a genuine incentive to change behavior rather than a concealment or default trap, a clear contrast with the Adobe renewal-email entry.

applications.title: Employees staying in their existing health plan after a major change to a large firm's insurance menu
applications.description: Handel uses a major change to insurance provision at a large (unnamed) firm to identify substantial inertia in employees' health plan choices, then estimates a choice model that quantifies risk preferences and ex ante health risk. He uses the estimates to simulate policies that nudge people toward better decisions by reducing inertia. This is an observational natural experiment plus a structural model, not a randomized trial.
applications.ethical_note: Inertia keeps people in plans that may no longer suit them, so reducing it looks helpful to each individual. The paper's modelled result is that doing so at scale can harm the market overall by worsening adverse selection, which is a real caution against assuming that nudging individuals toward better choices is automatically beneficial. These are model-based simulations, not an observed intervention, so they show a mechanism to be wary of rather than a measured harm.
